theme: By grace through faith; the new humanity; the mystery
readingInstruction: Read Ephesians 2:1-3:21. Chapter 2 is the gospel in miniature: dead, made alive, saved by grace, made one. Chapter 3 is about the mystery of the Gentiles’ inclusion and ends with a prayer and a doxology. Take time with 2:8-10 and 3:14-21.
settingTheScene: In chapter 1, Paul described what God has done in eternity and in Christ. In chapter 2, he describes what happened to us: we were dead, and God made us alive. Then he describes what happened between Jew and Gentile: the wall came down. Chapter 3 explains that this was the long-hidden mystery, and Paul’s calling is to proclaim it. The chapter closes with one of Paul’s greatest prayers.
observation: “And you were dead in the trespasses and sins” (2:1).
“But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ” (2:4-5).
“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (2:8-9).
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them” (2:10).
“That he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace” (2:15).
“This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel” (3:6).
“That you, being rooted and grounded in love, may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth” (3:17-18).

“Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us, to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever” (3:20-21).
interpretation:
The chapter begins with the worst news: “You were dead in the trespasses and sins in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air.” Dead is dead. Not sick, not weak, but dead. We were by nature children of wrath, carrying out the desires of the body and the mind. This is a bleak but accurate picture of humanity without Christ.

Then the two most beautiful words in the Bible: “But God.” “But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ.” The sequence is raising with Christ, seating with Christ. All of it is grace. “For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.” Faith itself is a gift. Salvation excludes boasting. Yet it is not for idleness: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them.” We are not saved by works, but we are saved for works. The word “workmanship” is poiema, from which we get “poem.” We are God’s work of art.

Verses 11 to 22 turn to the Gentiles, who were far off. “But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. For he himself is our peace.” The “dividing wall of hostility” may allude to the barrier in the temple that kept Gentiles out of the inner courts. Christ abolished the hostility and made one new humanity. This is a key text for understanding the relationship between Israel and the church: not replacement, but a new creation in which Jew and Gentile are united in one body under one Head.

In chapter 3, Paul speaks of the mystery: “that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel.” It was not made known in other generations as it has now been revealed. Paul has been given the grace to preach to the Gentiles “the unsearchable riches of Christ” and to make known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places the manifold wisdom of God through the church. Even angels learn about God by watching the church.

He bows his knees and prays: that God would strengthen them with power through his Spirit in the inner being, that Christ may dwell in their hearts through faith, that they being rooted and grounded in love may comprehend the breadth and length and height and depth, and know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, “that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.” It is a prayer for knowing what cannot be fully known. And then the doxology, to the God who can do more than we ask or think.
connection: Genesis 3 and Romans 5:12-21 explain our deadness in Adam. Romans 3:21-28 and Titus 3:3-7 teach salvation by grace. Isaiah 57:19 is cited in 2:17. Colossians 1:26-27 also speaks of the mystery. Romans 16:25-27 is a related doxology. Galatians 3:26-29 speaks of union of Jew and Gentile. John 15:5 and Colossians 3:3-4 speak of Christ in us. 1 Peter 1:10-12 says angels long to look into these things. Jude 24-25 is another doxology.
application:
Memorize Ephesians 2:8-10. Write it where you will see it.

Ask what “good works” God has prepared for you today, and look for one.

Pray Paul’s prayer of 3:16-19 for a friend or for your church.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for making you alive when you were dead in sin.
Thank him that you are saved by grace through faith, a gift.
Ask him to help you walk in the good works he prepared.
